'''William''' "'''Velvel'''" '''Morton Kahan''' (born June 5, 1933) is a [[Canadian]] [[mathematician]] and [[computer scientist]], who is a professor emeritus at [[University of California, Berkeley]]. He received the [[Turing Award]] in 1989 for "his fundamental contributions to [[numerical analysis]]."<ref name=TuringAward>{{cite web
  |url= https://amturing.acm.org/award_winners/kahan_1023746.cfm
  |title= William ("Velvel") Morton Kahan
  |last1= Haigh
  |first1= Thomas
  |date= 1989
  |website= A. M. Turing Award
  |access-date= 2017-05-27
}}</ref>

==Biography==
Born to a [[History of the Jews in Canada|Canadian Jewish]] family,<ref name=TuringAward/> he attended the [[University of Toronto]], where he received his bachelor's degree in 1954, his master's degree in 1956, and his Ph.D. in 1958, all in the field of mathematics. Kahan is now emeritus professor of mathematics and of electrical engineering and computer sciences (EECS) at the [[University of California, Berkeley]].

Kahan was the primary architect behind the [[IEEE 754-1985]] standard for [[floating-point]] computation (and its radix-independent follow-on, [[IEEE 854-1987|IEEE 854]]). He has been called "The Father of Floating Point", since he was instrumental in creating the original IEEE 754 specification.<ref name=TuringAward/> Kahan continued his contributions to the [[IEEE 754 revision]] that led to the current [[IEEE 754-2008|IEEE 754 standard]].

In the 1980s Kahan developed the program "paranoia", a benchmark that tests for a wide range of potential floating-point bugs.<ref>{{Citation
  |last1= Karpinski
  |first1= Richard
  |title = Paranoia: A floating-point benchmark
  |journal = Byte Magazine
  |year = 1985
  |volume = 10
  |issue = 2
  |pages = 223–235
  |url = https://archive.org/stream/byte-magazine-1985-02/1985_02_BYTE_10-02_Computing_and_the_Sciences#page/n222/mode/1up
}}</ref>  He also developed the [[Kahan summation algorithm]], an important algorithm for minimizing error introduced when adding a sequence of finite-precision [[floating-point number]]s.  He coined the term [[Rounding#Table-maker's_dilemma|"Table-maker's dilemma"]] for the unknown cost of correctly rounding [[transcendental function]]s to some preassigned number of digits.<ref>{{cite web |last=Kahan |first=William |title=A Logarithm Too Clever by Half |url=http://www.cs.berkeley.edu/~wkahan/LOG10HAF.TXT |access-date=2008-11-14}}</ref>

The [[Davis–Kahan–Weinberger dilation theorem]] is one of the landmark results in the dilation theory of [[Hilbert space]] operators and has found applications in many different areas.<ref>{{cite journal
  |last1= Davis
  |first1=Chandler
  |last2= Kahan
  |first2= W. M.
  |last3= Weinberger
  |first3= H. F.
  |title= Norm-Preserving Dilations and Their Applications to Optimal Error Bounds
  |journal= SIAM Journal on Numerical Analysis
  |volume= 19
  |issue= 3
  |pages= 445–469
  |doi= 10.1137/0719029
  |bibcode=1982SJNA...19..445D
  |year=1982
  |hdl=10338.dmlcz/128534
  |hdl-access= free
  }}</ref>

Kahan is an outspoken advocate of better education of the general computing population about floating-point issues and regularly denounces decisions in the design of computers and programming languages that he believes would impair good floating-point computations.<ref name=kahan_java>{{cite web | url=http://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~wkahan/JAVAhurt.pdf | title=How Java's Floating-Point Hurts Everyone Everywhere | date=1 March 1998 | last1=Kahan | first1=William | access-date=1 March 2021 }}</ref><ref name=kahan_interview>{{cite web | url=http://history.siam.org/%5C/pdfs2/Kahan_final.pdf | last1=Haigh | first1=Thomas | title=An interview with William M. Kahan | date=March 2016 | access-date=1 March 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=http://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~wkahan/MxMulEps.pdf | last1=Kahan | first1=William | title=Matlab's Loss is Nobody's Gain | access-date=1 March 2021 | date=31 July 2004}}</ref>

When [[Hewlett-Packard]] (HP) introduced the original [[HP-35]] pocket scientific calculator, its numerical accuracy in evaluating transcendental functions for some arguments was not optimal. HP worked extensively with Kahan to enhance the accuracy of the algorithms, which led to major improvements. This was documented at the time in the ''[[Hewlett-Packard Journal]]''.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Kahan |first=William M. |date=December 1979 |title=Personal Calculator Has Key to Solve Any Equation ''f''(''x'') = 0 |journal=Hewlett-Packard Journal |volume=30 |issue=12 |pages=20–26 |url=https://hparchive.com/Journals/HPJ-1979-12.pdf |access-date=2023-06-16 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Kahan |first=William M. |date=August 1980 |title=Handheld Calculator Evaluates Integrals |journal=Hewlett-Packard Journal |volume=31 |issue=8 |pages=23–32 |url=https://hparchive.com/Journals/HPJ-1980-08.pdf |access-date=2023-06-16 }}</ref>
He also contributed substantially to the design of the algorithms in the [[HP Voyager series]] and wrote part of their intermediate and advanced manuals.

Kahan was named an [[ACM Fellow]] in 1994, and inducted into the [[National Academy of Engineering]] in 2005.<ref name=TuringAward/>
